translations.text: In my first account, Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and teach.
until the day when, through the Holy Spirit, he gave instructions to the apostles whom he had chosen and was taken up.
After his suffering, he presented himself alive to them with many convincing proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.
While sharing bread with them, he instructed them not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father's promise, “which you heard from me.”
“For John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”
Those who had gathered asked him, “Lord, will you restore the kingdom to Israel at this time?”
He said to them, “It is not for you to know the times and seasons that the Father has established by his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, throughout Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”
When he had said this, he was taken up as they watched, and a cloud hid him from their sight.
While they were gazing in amazement toward heaven as he went, two men in white clothing appeared to them.
They said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking toward heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way that you saw him go into heaven.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called the Mount of Olives, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away.

When they entered, they went up to the upper room where they were staying: Peter and James, John and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.
All these continually joined together in prayer, along with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.
In those days Peter stood up among the brothers and said—the number of people gathered there was about a hundred and twenty—
“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled that the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus.
For he was numbered among us and had been allotted a share in this ministry.
He acquired a field with the wages of wrongdoing, and, swelling up, he burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out.
This became known to everyone living in Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.
For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let no one live in it,’ and, ‘Let another take his office.’
Therefore, from these men who accompanied us throughout the time when the Lord Jesus came and went among us,
beginning with John's baptism until the day when he was taken up from us, one must become a witness with us to his resurrection.”
They put forward two men: Joseph, who was called Barsabbas and was also named Justus, and Matthias.
They prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know everyone's heart, reveal which one of these two you have chosen.”
to receive a share in this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas fell away to go to his own place.
They cast lots for them, and the lot fell to Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in unity.
Suddenly a sound came from heaven like a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting.
And divided tongues, as if of fire, appeared to them, and one rested on each of them.
And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit enabled them to speak.
Now there were Jews living in Jerusalem, devout men from every nation under heaven.
When this sound arose, the crowd gathered together and was bewildered, because each person heard them speaking in his own language.
They were all amazed and astonished and said to one another, “Are not all these people who are speaking Galileans?
And how do we each hear them in our own native language?
Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those living in Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, and Asia,
in Phrygia and Pamphylia, in Egypt and the regions of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
both Jews and converts to their faith, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own languages about the mighty deeds of God.”
They were all amazed and perplexed and said to one another, “What can this mean?”
But some mocked them and said, “They must be full of sweet wine.”
Then Peter stood up with the eleven, raised his voice, and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who live in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words.
These people are not drunk, as you suppose, for it is only the third hour of the day.
Rather, this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel:
‘And after this, in the last days, says God, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy, your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.
And on my male servants and my female servants I will pour out my Spirit in those days, and they will prophesy.
And I will give signs in heaven above and signs on earth below: blood and fire and swirling smoke.
The sun will turn to darkness and the moon to blood before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes.
And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’
Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth was a man whom God attested to you through mighty deeds, signs, and wonders that God performed through him among you, as you yourselves know.
He was handed over according to God's determined plan and foreknowledge, and you nailed him to a tree by the hands of lawless men and killed him.
God raised him up, releasing him from the pains of death, because it was impossible for him to be held by it.
For David says about him, ‘I always saw the Lord before me, for he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken.
Therefore my heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced; my body too will dwell in hope.
For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your Holy One see decay.
You have made known to me the paths of life; you have filled me with joy through the sweetness of your presence.
Men and brothers, we may speak freely about the patriarch David: he both died and was buried, and his tomb remains among us to this day.
He was a prophet and knew that God had sworn an oath to him to seat one of his descendants on his throne.
Foreseeing this, he spoke about the resurrection of Christ: his soul was not left in Hades, nor did his body undergo decay.
God raised this Jesus, and we are all witnesses to this.
Exalted at God's right hand and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this which you yourselves see and hear.
For David did not ascend into heaven, but he himself says, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand,
until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’”
Therefore let the whole house of Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Anointed One.
When they heard this, they felt remorse in their hearts and said to Peter and the other apostles, “What shall we do, men and brothers?”
Peter said to them, “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the promise of the Holy Spirit.
For the promise is for you and your children, and for all who are far away, whom the Lord our God will call.”
With many other words he bore witness and encouraged them, saying, “Be saved from this crooked generation.”
Some gladly received his word and were baptized, and about three thousand people were added that day.
They devoted themselves continually to the apostles' teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayers.
Awe and fear came upon everyone, and many signs and mighty works were performed through the apostles.
All the believers were together and held everything in common.
They sold their possessions and belongings and distributed the proceeds to everyone according to each person's need.
Every day they went early to the temple in unity, broke bread in their homes, and ate their food with joy and sincerity of heart.
They praised God and enjoyed favor with all the people, and every day the Lord added those who were being saved to their company.
Peter and John were going up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer.
There was a man lame from his mother's womb, who was carried and placed every day at the temple gate called Beautiful to ask for alms from those entering the temple.
When he saw Peter and John entering the temple, he begged to receive alms.
Peter, together with John, looked intently at him and said, “Look at us.”
He turned toward them, expecting to receive something from them.
And Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk.”
And taking him by the right hand, he raised him up, and immediately his feet and legs became strong.
He sprang up and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
And all the people saw him walking and praising God.
And they recognized him as the one who used to sit asking for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with amazement at the miraculous sign that had taken place.
And while he held on to Peter and John, all the people ran to them in the portico called Solomon’s, amazed.
When Peter saw this, he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why are you amazed at this, or why do you stare at us as though we had made him walk by our own power or prowess?
The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his Son Jesus, whom you handed over and denied before Pilate, when he had decided to release him.
But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a man condemned to death be granted to you.
And you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. We ourselves are witnesses to this.
And through faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. And the faith that comes through him has given him this complete health before you all.
And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers.
But what God foretold through the mouths of all the prophets—that his Christ would suffer—he has fulfilled in this way.
Therefore repent and turn back, so that your sins may be erased,
so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and he may send Jesus Christ, who was appointed beforehand for you.
Heaven must receive him until the time for the restoration of all things of which God spoke through the mouths of his holy prophets.
Moses said to our fathers, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. Listen to him in everything he says to you.
And every person who does not listen to that prophet will be destroyed from among the people.’
And all the prophets who spoke from Samuel onward also foretold these days.
You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘In your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed.’
God raised up his Son and sent him to you first, to bless you by turning each of you away from your wicked ways.”
And while they were speaking to the people, the priests, the officers of the temple, and the Sadducees came upon them,
angry because they were teaching the people and proclaiming through Jesus the resurrection of the dead.
They laid their hands on them and put them in prison until the next day, for it was already evening.
But many of those who heard the message believed, and the number of men came to about five thousand.
The next day, their rulers, elders, and scribes gathered in Jerusalem,
along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who belonged to the priestly family.
They brought them forward and asked, “By what power or by what name have you done this?”
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders of Israel,
if it is right to question us today about a good deed done to a disabled man and about how he was healed,

let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that it is in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands here before you healed.
He is the stone rejected by you builders, which became the cornerstone.
There is salvation through no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.”
Seeing the boldness of Peter and John and realizing that they were uneducated men without formal learning, they were amazed, for they recognized that they had been with Jesus.
They also saw the healed man standing with them and could say nothing in reply.
After ordering them to leave the council, they discussed the matter among themselves,
saying, “What shall we do with these men? A remarkable sign has been performed through them, which is known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.
But so that it spreads no further among the people, let us threaten them not to speak to anyone anymore in that name.”
They called them in and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, “Judge whether it is right before God to listen to you rather than to God.
For we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
After threatening them, they released them, finding no way to punish them because of the people, since everyone was glorifying God for what had happened.
For the man on whom this sign of healing had been performed was more than forty years old.
After being released, they went to their own people and reported everything the chief priests and elders had said to them.
When they heard this, they raised their voices to God and said, “You, Lord God, made heaven, earth, the sea, and everything in them.
Through the Holy Spirit, you said by the mouth of our father David, your servant, ‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?
The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Anointed One.’
For truly, in this city, Herod and Pontius Pilate gathered with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed,
to do everything that your hand and your will had determined beforehand would happen.
And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant your servants to speak your word with all boldness,
as you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders take place through the name of your holy Son Jesus.”
While they were praying, the place where they were gathered shook, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God boldly.
The multitude of believers were of one heart and soul, and none of them said that any of their possessions belonged to them alone, but they held everything in common.
And with great power the apostles testified to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ, and great grace was upon them all.
And no one among them was in need, for all who owned lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what they had sold.
They laid them at the apostles’ feet, and they distributed them to each person according to their need.
Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, which means “son of encouragement,” was a Levite, a Cypriot by birth.
He owned a field, sold it, and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a farm.
And he kept back some of the money, with his wife’s knowledge, and brought a portion and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart so that you lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back some of the money from the field?
Was it not yours while it remained unsold? And after it was sold, was the money not under your control? Why have you put this deed in your heart? You have not lied to human beings but to God.”
When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last, and great fear came upon all who heard about it.
The young men rose, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.
About three hours passed, and his wife came in, not knowing what had happened.
Peter addressed her and said, “Tell me, did you sell the field for this much?” And she said, “Yes, for that much.”
And Peter said to her, “Why have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Look, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out too.”
Immediately she fell at his feet and breathed her last. The young men came in, found her dead, and carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard about it.
Through the hands of the apostles, many signs and wonders took place among the people, and they were all together with one accord in Solomon’s Portico.
None of the others dared to join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
And more and more believers in the Lord were added, a multitude of men and women.
so that they even brought the sick out into the streets and laid them on stretchers and beds, so that as Peter passed by, at least his shadow might fall on some of them.
A crowd also gathered in Jerusalem from the surrounding towns, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
The high priest rose up, and all those with him, who belonged to the sect of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy.
And they seized the apostles and put them in the public prison.
Then an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors during the night, led them out, and said:
“Go, stand in the temple, and speak to the people all the words of this life.”

When they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began teaching. The high priest and those with him came and called together the council and the whole assembly of elders of the people of Israel, and they sent to the prison to have them brought.
But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported:
“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside.”
When the temple officers and the chief priests heard these words, they were perplexed about them, wondering what would come of this.
Then someone came and told them, “Look, the men you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”
Then the captain went with the officers and brought them back, but not by force, because they were afraid the people would stone them.
They brought them in and stood them before the council. The high priest questioned them
and said, “Did we not strictly command you not to teach in that name? Yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you want to bring that man’s blood upon us.”
Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than human beings.
The God of our ancestors raised up Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him by his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give Israel repentance and forgiveness of sins.
We are witnesses of these things, as is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”
When they heard this, they were enraged and planned to kill them.
But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law respected by all the people, stood up in the council and ordered that the men be taken outside for a little while.
He said to them, “Men of Israel, consider carefully what you ought to do with these men.
Before these days, Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about four hundred men joined him. He was killed, and all who had joined him were scattered and came to nothing.
After him, Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and led many people in rebellion after him. He too perished, and all who had followed him were scattered.
Now I tell you: keep away from these men and leave them alone, because if this plan or undertaking is of human origin, it will fall apart.
But if it is from God, you cannot overthrow them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.”
They agreed with him. They called in the apostles, flogged them, ordered them not to speak any more in the name of Jesus, and released them.
They left the council rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name.
Every day, in the temple and in people’s homes, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the good news of Jesus Christ.
In those days, as the disciples grew in number, the Greeks complained against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution.
The Twelve called together the whole body of disciples and said, “It is not right for us to leave the word of God to serve tables.
Brothers, choose seven men of good reputation from among you, whom we will appoint to oversee these needs.”
But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.
This proposal pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a convert from Antioch.
They presented them before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
The word of God spread, and the number of disciples increased greatly in Jerusalem. A large number of priests also became obedient to the faith.
Stephen, a man full of grace and power, performed wonders and great signs among the people.
Some from the assembly called that of the Libyans, Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and those from Cilicia and Asia, rose to argue with Stephen.
They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.
Then they induced some men to say, “We heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.”
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, came upon him, seized him, and brought him before the council.
They presented false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law.”
We heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the laws that Moses gave us.
Everyone sitting in the council looked intently at him and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
The high priest said, “Is this really so?”
He said, “Brothers and fathers, listen to me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he had been settled in Haran, and said to him,
‘Leave your land and your kindred, and come to the land that I will show you.’
Then he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God moved him from there and made him live as a stranger in this land where you now live.
He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s breadth, but promised to give it to him as a dwelling place and to his descendants after him, though he had no son.
God spoke this way: ‘His descendants will be strangers in a foreign land, and they will be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.
But I will judge the nation they serve,’ says God, ‘and afterward they will come out and worship me in this place.’
He gave him the covenant of circumcision. Then Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt, but God was with him.
He rescued him from all his troubles and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, who appointed him ruler over the Egyptians and over his entire household.
A famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and there was great distress. Our fathers could find no food.
When Jacob heard that food could be found in Egypt, he sent our fathers there for the first time.
On the second visit, Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and his family became known to Pharaoh.
Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people.
Jacob went down to Egypt, and he and our fathers died there.
They were brought to Shechem and laid in the cave that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.
As the time drew near for the promise God had made to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied greatly in Egypt,
until another king arose in Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He dealt deceitfully with our people and oppressed our ancestors, making them abandon their infants so that they would not survive.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in God's sight. He was brought up in his father's house for three months.
When he was abandoned, Pharaoh's daughter took him in and brought him up as her own son.
Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in his words and deeds.
When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel.
When he saw someone being mistreated, he became angry and avenged the victim by killing the Egyptian.
He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was going to give them deliverance through him, but they did not understand.
The next day he appeared among them while they were fighting and tried to bring them to peace, saying, “Men, you are brothers. Why do you mistreat one another?”
But the man who was mistreating his neighbor pushed him away and said, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”
At these words Moses fled and became a foreign resident in the land of Midian, where he had two sons.
When forty years had passed, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush.
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight. As he approached to look more closely, the voice of the Lord came:
“I am the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” Moses was struck with fear and did not dare to look.
The Lord said to him, “Take the sandals off your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.
I have indeed seen the suffering of my people in Egypt and heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. Now come, and I will send you to Egypt.”
This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?”—God sent him as ruler and deliverer through the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
He led them out, performing signs and wonders in the land of the Egyptians, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the children of Israel, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. Listen to him.”
This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers, and who received living words to give to us.
Our ancestors were unwilling to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and turned back to Egypt in their hearts.
They said to Aaron, “Make us gods who will go before us, because we do not know what has happened to that Moses who brought us out of the land of the Egyptians.”
In those days they made a calf, offered sacrifices to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.

But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: “Did you offer me sacrifices and offerings for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, the images you made to worship. I will deport you beyond the land of the Babylonians.”
Our ancestors had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, just as the one who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern he had seen.
Our ancestors received it and brought it with Joshua into the land possessed by the nations whom God drove out before our ancestors. It remained there until the days of David.
who found favor before God and asked to find dwelling places for the God of Jacob.
And Solomon built a house for him.
But the Most High does not dwell in temples made by human hands, as the prophet says:
“Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what place will be my resting place?
Did not my hand make all these things?”
You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit. You are just like your fathers.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, whom you have now betrayed and murdered.
You received the law at the direction of angels, but did not keep it.
When they heard this, they were enraged in their hearts and gnashed their teeth at him.

But he was full of the Holy Spirit, looked up into heaven, and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand. He said, “Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand.”
They shouted with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed at him together.
They drove him outside the city and stoned him. The witnesses laid their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They stoned Stephen as he called out and said, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
He knelt down and cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep. And Saul approved of his killing.
On that day a great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem, and everyone except the apostles was scattered throughout the countryside of Judea and Samaria.
Devout men carried Stephen away and made great lamentation over him.
But Saul was devastating the church. He went from house to house, dragged off men and women, and handed them over to prison.
Those who had been scattered went about proclaiming the good news of the word.
Philip went down to the city of the Samaritans and proclaimed Christ to them.
The crowds paid close attention together to Philip's words as they heard him and saw the signs he performed.
For unclean spirits came out of many who had them, crying out with a loud voice.
And many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
And there was great joy in that city. A man named Simon had previously been practicing magic in the city and astonishing the Samaritan people, claiming that he was someone great.
Everyone, from the least to the greatest, paid attention to him and said, “This man is the power of God that is called Great.”
They paid attention to him because he had astonished them with his magic for a long time.
But when they believed Philip, who preached the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were all baptized, both men and women.
Simon himself also believed, and after being baptized he stayed close to Philip. When he saw the signs and great miracles that were taking place, he was amazed.
When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria too had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
They went down and prayed for them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit.
For until then he had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money and said,
“Give me this authority too, so that whoever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain God’s gift with money.
You have no part or share in this matter, because your heart is not upright before God.
Repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord, so that perhaps you may be forgiven for the [?] thoughts of your heart.
For I see that you are in the bitterness of gall and in the bonds of unrighteousness.”
Simon answered, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that none of the things you have spoken of may come upon me.”
After giving testimony and speaking the word of God, they returned to Jerusalem and preached the good news in many Samaritan villages.
An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip and said, “Get up and go south along the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza, for this is a desert road.”
He got up and went. And there was an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasury. He had come to Jerusalem to worship,
and was returning, seated in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go over and stay close to that chariot.”
Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah. He said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he asked Philip to come up and sit with him.
The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: “He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth.
In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. And who will recount his lineage? For his life is taken away from the earth.”
The eunuch said to Philip, “Please tell me, about whom does the prophet say this—about himself or about someone else?”
Philip opened his mouth and, beginning with this Scripture, told him the good news about Jesus.
As they traveled along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?”
And he said to him, “If you believe with all your heart, you may.” He answered, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”
And he ordered the chariot to stop, and both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and he baptized him.
And when they came up out of the water, the Holy Spirit came upon the eunuch, and an angel of the Lord snatched Philip away. The eunuch saw him no more and went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip was found at Azotus, and as he traveled he preached the good news to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
But Saul, still full of threats and murderous intent against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest.
He asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found anyone belonging to that Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
And as he traveled and drew near Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”
And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
“But get up and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do.”
The men traveling with him stood speechless; they heard only the voice but saw nothing.
Saul got up from the ground, and although his eyes were open, he could see no one. They took him by the hand and led him into Damascus.
And he was there for three days, unable to see, and he neither ate nor drank.
There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.”
And the Lord said to him, “Get up and go along the street called Straight, and inquire at Judas’s house for a man named Saul, from Tarsus, for he is still praying.”
“And in a vision he saw a man named Ananias come in and lay his hand on him so that he might see.”
Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many people about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem.”
“And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind everyone who calls upon your name.”
The Lord said to him, “Go, for he is my chosen instrument to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel.”
“For I myself will show him how much he must suffer for my name.”

And Ananias went and entered the house, laid his hands on him, and said, “Brother Saul, look up. The Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming, has sent me so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he could see. He got up and was baptized.
After taking food, he regained his strength, and he stayed with the disciples in Damascus for some days.
And immediately he preached Jesus in the synagogues, saying that he is the Son of God.

All who heard him were amazed and said, “Was this not the man who wreaked havoc in Jerusalem among those who called on the name of Jesus? And he has come here for that very purpose, to take them bound to the chief priests.”
But Saul grew stronger still and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus, demonstrating that Jesus is the Christ.
When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him.
Their plot became known to Saul, for they were watching the gates day and night so that they could kill him.
And the disciples took him by night and lowered him in a basket over the wall.
When Saul came to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him and did not believe that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. He told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road, how the Lord had spoken to him, and how he had spoken boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus.
And he was with them, going in and out of Jerusalem, speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
He spoke and debated with the Greeks, and they planned to kill him.
When the brothers learned of this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus.
But the church throughout all Judea, Samaria, and Galilee had peace and was built up. It walked in the fear of the Lord and grew in number through the encouragement of the Holy Spirit.
As Peter traveled among them all, he also went down to the saints who lived in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas, who was paralyzed and had lain in bed for eight years.
Peter said to him, “Aeneas, the Lord Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and shake out your bedding yourself.” And he got up immediately.
All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.
In Joppa there was a woman disciple named Tabitha, which in translation is called Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity that she performed.
In those days she became ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upstairs room there.
Lydda was near Joppa. When the disciples heard that Peter was there, they sent two men to him, begging him not to delay coming to them.
Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him to the upstairs room. All the widows stood around him, weeping and showing him the clothing and garments that Dorcas had made for them.

Peter sent everyone outside, knelt down, and prayed. Then he turned toward the body and said, “Tabitha, get up in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.” She opened her eyes and, seeing Peter, sat upright.
He gave her his hand and helped her up. He called the saints and the widows and presented her to them alive.
This became known throughout Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
He stayed in Joppa for many days with a certain Simon, a tanner.
There was a man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of the regiment called the Italian Regiment.
He was devout and feared God with his entire household, gave many alms to the people, and prayed to God at all times.
At the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him and saying, “Cornelius!”
He stared at him in fear and said, “What is it, Lord?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your acts of charity have risen as a memorial before God.”
Now send men to Joppa and summon a certain Simon who is called Peter.
He is staying with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is near the sea.
When the angel who had spoken with him departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among his attendants.
He told them everything and sent them to Joppa.
The next day, while they were traveling and approaching the city, Peter went up onto the rooftop to pray at the sixth hour.
He became hungry and wanted to eat. While they were preparing the food, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet suspended by its four corners, descending and settling on the ground.
In it were all kinds of four-footed animals, creeping creatures of the earth, and birds of the sky.
A voice came to him: “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.”
Peter said, “Certainly not, Lord, for I have never eaten anything defiled or unclean.”
A voice came to him a second time: “What God has made clean, you must not make unclean.”
This happened twice, and the vessel was taken up into heaven.
While Peter was wondering in his mind what the vision he had seen might mean, the men sent by Cornelius asked for Simon’s house and stood at the gate.
They called out and asked whether Simon, who was called Peter, was staying there.
While Peter was thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Look, some men are looking for you.
Get up, go down, and go with them without any hesitation, because I have sent them.”
When Peter went down to them, he said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason you have come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man who fears God and is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was instructed by a holy angel to invite you to his house and hear what you have to say.”
He invited them inside and gave them lodging. The next day Peter got up and went with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went with him.
The following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and close friends.
As Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and worshiped him.
But Peter raised him up and said, “Stand up. I myself am also a man.”
Talking with him, he went inside and found many people gathered there.

He said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jewish man to associate with or approach someone of another nation. But God has shown me that I must not call any person defiled or unclean.
For this reason I came when invited, without raising any objection. Now I ask: Why did you send for me?”
Cornelius said, “Four days ago, at this hour, I was praying at the ninth hour in my house, and suddenly a man came and stood before me in white clothing and said,
‘Cornelius, your prayers have been heard, and your acts of charity have been remembered before God.
Now send to Joppa and invite Simon, who is called Peter. He is staying in the house of Simon, a [?], near the sea. He will come and speak with you.’
So I sent for you immediately, and you have done well to come. Now we are all here before God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you.”
Peter opened his mouth and said, “I have truly come to understand that God shows no partiality,
but in every nation, whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.
He sent the message to the children of Israel, proclaiming the good news of peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all.
You yourselves know what happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed:
how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power. He went about doing good and healing all who were held captive by Satan, because God was with him.
We are witnesses of everything he did in the land of Judea and in Jerusalem. They killed him by hanging him on a tree.
God raised him on the third day and allowed him to appear,
not to all the people, but to us, the witnesses chosen beforehand by God, who ate and drank with him after his resurrection from the dead.
And he commanded us to preach to the people and testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.
All the prophets testify about him that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.
While Peter was speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came upon everyone who was listening to the message.
The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were amazed that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were being poured out on the Gentiles too.
For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God.
Then Peter answered, “Can anyone withhold water and prevent these people from being baptized, since they have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?”
And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay there for a few days.
The apostles and the brothers who were in the regions of Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.
But when Peter went up to Jerusalem, the circumcised believers criticized him,
saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”
Peter began explaining it to them in order, saying,
“I was praying in the city of Joppa, and in a trance I saw a vision: something like a large sheet was coming down, suspended from heaven by its four corners, and it came right down to me.
I looked closely into it and saw four-footed animals of the earth, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds of the sky.
And I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter; kill and eat.’
But I said, ‘Certainly not, Lord, for nothing defiled or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’
The voice from heaven answered me a second time, ‘What God has made clean, you must not consider defiled.’
This happened three times, and everything was taken back up into heaven.
And just then three men arrived and stood at the house where I was, having been sent to me from Caesarea.
The Spirit told me to go with them without hesitation. These six brothers also came with me, and we entered that man’s house.
He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter.
He will speak words to you by which you and your entire household will be saved.’
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit came upon them, just as upon us at the beginning.
I remembered the Lord’s words, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
So then, if God gave them the same gift as he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, how could I stand in God’s way?”
When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.”
Those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose against Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.
But some of them were men from Cyprus and Cyrene who, on entering Antioch, spoke to the Greeks, proclaiming the good news of the Lord Jesus.
The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number of those who believed turned to the Lord.
News about them reached the ears of the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas as far as Antioch.
When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to remain with the Lord with willing hearts.
For he was a cheerful-hearted man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great many people were added to the Lord.
He went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he found him, he brought him to Antioch.
For a whole year they gathered with the church and taught a great many people, and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that there would be a great famine throughout the whole world. This happened under Claudius.
The disciples, each according to what he could afford, decided to send help for the needs of the brothers who lived in Judea.
And they did so, sending it to the elders through Barnabas and Saul.
At that time King Herod laid hands on some members of the church to mistreat them.
He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter as well. These were the days of Unleavened Bread.
After arresting him, he put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him, intending to bring him before the people after Passover.
Peter was kept under guard in prison, and the church frequently offered prayers to God for him.
On the night when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and guards in front of the door were watching over the prison.
Suddenly an angel of the Lord came and stood beside him, and a light shone in the room. He struck Peter’s side, woke him, and said, “Get up quickly!” And the chains fell from his hands.
The angel said to him, “Put on your belt and put your sandals on your feet.” He did so. Then he said to him, “Put on your cloak and follow me.”
He went out and followed him, not knowing that what the angel was doing was real, for he thought he was seeing a dream.

When they had passed the first guard and the second, they came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them by itself, and they went through and along one street. Immediately the angel left him.
When Peter came to his senses, he said, “Now I know for certain that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s hands and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
After considering this, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many people were gathered and praying.
When he knocked at the doors of the house, a servant girl named Rhoda came to listen.
Recognizing Peter’s voice, she was so happy that she did not open the door, but ran inside and announced that Peter was standing at the door.
They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she kept insisting that it was so, and they said, “It must be his angel.”
Peter kept knocking. When they opened the door, they saw him and were astonished.
He motioned with his hand for them to be quiet and told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison. He said, “Tell James and the brothers about this.” Then he left and went to another place.
When day came, there was great commotion among the soldiers over what could have happened to Peter.
When Herod searched for him and did not find him, he questioned the guards and ordered them to be put to death. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together and, after winning over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, asked for peace, because their country received its food from the king’s country.
On a notable day, Herod put on his royal robes, sat on the judgment seat, and addressed them publicly.
The crowd shouted, “This is the voice of a god, not of a man!”
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give glory to God, and he became infested with worms and died.
The word of God grew and spread.
Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem after completing their service, taking with them John, who was called Mark.
In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
While they were serving the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and sent them away.
Sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus.
When they reached Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. They also had John as their assistant.
After traveling through the whole island as far as Paphos, they found there a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. The proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul and wanted to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the magician—for that is how his name is translated—opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him
and said, “You who are full of all deceit and cunning, son of Satan, enemy of all righteousness, will you not stop twisting the Lord’s straight paths?
Now, look, the Lord’s hand is upon you, and you will be blind, unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about looking for people to lead him.
Then, when the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Paul and his companions sailed from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John left them and returned to Jerusalem.
They went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. On the Sabbath day they entered the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent word to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any words of encouragement for the people, speak.”
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said, ‘Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen.’
The God of this people Israel chose our ancestors and exalted the people during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm he brought them out of there.
And for about forty years he fed them in the wilderness.
And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance for about four hundred and fifty years.
And after this he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet.
Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
And when he removed him, he raised up David as their king, concerning whom he also testified, saying, “I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will carry out all my wishes.”
From this man's descendants, God, according to his promise, raised up Jesus as Savior for Israel,
in accordance with John's earlier preaching of a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel before his arrival.
And as John was completing his course, he said, “Who do you think I am? I am not he. But look, someone is coming after me whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.”
Brothers, descendants of Abraham's family, and those among you who fear God, this message of salvation has been sent to you.
But those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize him, and by condemning him they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every Sabbath.
And although they found no grounds for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him killed.
And when they had carried out everything that was written about him, they took him down from the wood and laid him in a tomb.
But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those
who had gone up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people.
And we bring you the good news of the promise made to our ancestors,
because God has fulfilled it for us, their children, by raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm: “You are my Son; today I have fathered you.”
And concerning his raising him from the dead, never again to return to decay, he says this: “I will give you the holy, faithful blessings of David.”
For he also says in another passage, ‘You will not let your Holy One see decay.’
But David served in his own generation, fell asleep according to God's will, was gathered to his ancestors, and experienced decay.
But the one whom God raised did not see decay.
Let it be known to you, brothers, that through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you,
and everyone who believes is justified through him from everything from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses.
Be careful, lest what was spoken in the prophets come upon you:
“Look, you scoffers, marvel and be destroyed, for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe even if someone tells you about it.”
And as they went out from there, they begged that these same words be spoken to them on the next Sabbath.
And when the assembly was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke with them and persuaded them to remain in the grace of God.
On the next Sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God.
When the Jews saw the crowd, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what Paul said, speaking abusively.

Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly and said, “The word of God had to be spoken to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, look, we are turning to the Gentiles.”
“For this is what the Lord commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.’”
When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and those who had been appointed to eternal life believed.
And the word of God spread throughout the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the devout, respectable women and the leading men of the city. They raised a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their territory.
They shook the dust off their feet against them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.
In Iconium they entered the Jewish synagogue together and spoke in such a way that a very large number of both Jews and Greeks believed.
But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and turned their minds against the brothers.
They remained there for a long time, speaking boldly, while the Lord bore witness to the word of his grace by granting that signs and wonders should be done through their hands.
The people of the city were divided: some sided with the Jews and others with the apostles.
When the Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, made a move to mistreat and stone them,
they learned of it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding countryside, and they preached the good news there.
A man from Lystra sat there with weak feet. He had been lame from his mother’s womb and had never walked.
He listened to Paul’s words. Paul looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed.
He said in a loud voice, “I say to you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, stand upright on your feet!” And he began leaping and walking.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices and said in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in human likeness!”
They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
The priest of Zeus, who was before the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gate and wanted to offer sacrifices together with the crowds.
When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and ran out of the crowd, shouting

and saying, “Men, why are you doing this? We too are human beings with the same weaknesses as you. We bring you the good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them.”
“In past generations he allowed all the Gentiles to follow their own ways.”
“Yet he did not leave himself without a witness: he did good by giving you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and joy.”
Even after saying this, they could barely quiet the crowds so that they would not sacrifice to them but would instead go back to their own places.

While they were going about and teaching, Jews came from Antioch and Iconium. By arguing boldly, they persuaded the people to turn away from them, saying, “They speak no truth at all; everything they say is a lie.” They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead.
But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and entered the city. The next morning he left for Derbe with Barnabas.
After preaching the gospel in that city and making many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to remain firm in the faith, saying, “We must enter the kingdom of God through many hardships.”
They appointed elders for them in each church, and after praying with fasting, they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
They traveled through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia.
After speaking the word of the Lord in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
From there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
When they arrived and gathered the church together, they reported all that God had done through them and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
They spent a considerable time with the disciples.
Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the laws of Moses, you cannot be saved.”

After considerable disagreement and debate arose between Paul and Barnabas and these men, they decided that Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them should go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this question.
Sent on their way by the church, they traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, reporting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers.
When they reached Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church, the apostles, and the elders, and they reported all that God had done through them.
But some believers from the sect of the Pharisees stood up and said, “They must be circumcised and commanded to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and elders gathered to consider this matter.

After much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you yourselves know that in the early days God chose, in your midst, that the Gentiles should hear the message of the gospel through my mouth and believe.
God, who knows the heart, testified on their behalf by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us.
He made no distinction between them and us, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Now why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the necks of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
Rather, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are.”
The whole assembly fell silent and listened to Barnabas and Paul recount all the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
After they finished speaking, James responded, saying, “Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name.
The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
After this I will return and rebuild David’s fallen tent. I will rebuild its ruins and raise it up,
so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, along with all the nations over whom my name has been called, says the Lord, who does all these things.
It has been known from eternity.
Therefore I judge that we should not trouble those among the Gentiles who turn to God,
but write to them to keep away from food offered to idols, from sexual immorality, from the flesh of animals that have died, and from blood.
For from the earliest generations Moses has had those who proclaim him in every city, and he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath.

Then the apostles and elders, together with the whole church, thought it good to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men.
They wrote this to the brothers and sent it through them: ‘The apostles, elders, and brothers send greetings to you brothers from among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia.’

For we have heard that some people, claiming to come from us, troubled you with their words and unsettled your souls, saying that you must be circumcised and keep the law, though we gave them no such instruction.
It seemed good to us, having gathered in agreement, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have given up their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So we have sent Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to place no further burden on you beyond these necessary things:
to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. Farewell.
So they were sent off and went down to Antioch, where they gathered the people and delivered the letter.
When they read it, they rejoiced at its encouragement.
Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words.
After spending some time there, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to return to the apostles.
But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.
Paul and Barnabas went about in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the word of the Lord, along with many others.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas wanted to take John, who was called Mark, as well.
But Paul urged them not to take along the man who had left them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.
There was a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from one another. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and departed, having been entrusted by the brothers to the grace of God.
He traveled through the regions of Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
He came to Derbe and Lystra. There was a disciple there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Gentile father.
who was well spoken of by the brothers in Lystra and Iconium.
Paul wanted to take him along, so he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Gentile.
As they passed through the cities, they handed on to them the decrees issued by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to observe.
The churches were strengthened in faith and increased in number every day.
They traveled through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
When they reached Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.
Passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.
A vision appeared to Paul during the night: a Macedonian man stood pleading with him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to leave for Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to proclaim the good news to them.
Setting out from Troas, we sailed straight to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis,
and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a colony. We stayed in that city for several days.
On the Sabbath day we went outside the city to the riverbank, where prayers were thought to be offered. We sat down and spoke with the women who had gathered.
A woman named Lydia, a seller of purple cloth from the city of Thyatira who worshiped God, listened. The Lord himself opened her heart to attend to Paul's words.
When she and her household were baptized, she pleaded with us, saying, “If you consider me faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” She insisted and took us with her.
As we were going to prayer, we met a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her masters much profit by fortune-telling.
She followed Paul and us, crying out and saying, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who tell you the way of salvation.”
She did this for many days. Paul became angry, turned, and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.
When her masters saw that their hope of profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the authorities.
They brought them before the magistrates and said, “These men are throwing our city into turmoil. They are Jews
and teach us customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans.”
The crowd gathered against them, and the magistrates tore their own clothes and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
After inflicting many wounds on them, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them securely.
Having received such an order, he put them in the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.
At midnight Paul and Silas were praying and praising God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison shook. Immediately all the doors opened, and everyone's bonds came loose.
When the jailer woke and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to take his own life, thinking that the prisoners had escaped.
Paul called out in a loud voice, saying, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here!”
He asked for a light, rushed inside, and, seized with fear, fell down before Paul and Silas.
He brought them outside and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your whole household.”
They spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house.
He took them at that very hour of the night and washed their wounds, and immediately he and all his people were baptized there.
He brought them into his house and set food before them, and rejoiced with his whole household because he had believed in God.
When morning came, the magistrates sent their officers, saying, “Release those men.”
The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders for you to be released. Now come out and go in peace.”

But Paul said to them, “They beat us publicly, though we are innocent men and Romans, and threw us into prison. And now are they sending us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and bring us out.”
The officers reported these words to the magistrates. They were seized with fear when they heard that they were Romans, and came and pleaded with them.
After bringing them out, they begged them to leave the city.
They left the prison and went to Lydia. When they saw the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
After traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As was his custom, Paul went in to them and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures.
He explained and set before them that Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that “This Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ.”
Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a very large number of God-worshiping Gentiles and not a few of the leading women.
The Jews became jealous, took some wicked men from the rabble, gathered a mob, and threw the city into turmoil. They rushed to Jason’s house and sought to bring them out into the public square.
When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city officials, crying out, “These men who have thrown the world into turmoil have come here too!
Jason has welcomed them, and they all act against Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”
They stirred up the crowd and the city officials who heard these things.
After taking a guarantee from Jason and the others, they released them.
The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. When they arrived there, they went to the Jewish synagogue.
These people were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica. They received the word with complete eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Many of them believed, as did not a few respectable Greek women and men.
But when the Jews in Thessalonica learned that the word of God had also been proclaimed by Paul in Berea, they came there too, stirring up and troubling the crowds.
Then the brothers immediately sent Paul away to go to the coast, while Silas and Timothy remained there.
Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. After receiving instructions for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him because he saw that the city was given over to idolatry.
He spoke in the synagogue with the Jews and the worshipers, and in the marketplace every day with those he happened to meet.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers argued with him. Some said, “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign gods,” because he was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.
They took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “Can we learn what this new teaching is that you are proclaiming?
You are bringing some strange things to our ears, and we want to know what these things mean.”
For all the Athenians and the foreigners staying there spent their time on nothing else but telling or hearing something new.
Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that you are very religious in every respect.
For as I walked around and looked at the objects of your worship, I found an altar on which was written, ‘To an unknown God.’ What you worship without knowing, I proclaim to you.
The God who made the world and everything in it is Lord of heaven and earth and does not dwell in temples made by human hands.
Nor is he served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything.

From one blood he made every nation of humanity to dwell over the whole face of the earth. He established their appointed times and the boundaries of their dwelling places, so that they would seek God,
in the hope that they might feel their way toward him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.
For in him we live and move and exist, as some of your own poets have also said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’
Since we are God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone carved by human skill and imagination.
God overlooked the times of ignorance, but now he commands all people to repent.
For he has established a day on which he is to judge the world in righteousness through the man whom he appointed, giving assurance to everyone by raising him from the dead.”
When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, while others said, “We will hear you about this another time.”
Then Paul left their midst and went away.
But some people joined him and believed. Among them were Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After this, Paul left Athens and came to Corinth.
He found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, and he joined them.
Because he practiced the same trade, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
He spoke in the synagogue every Sabbath and persuaded Jews and Gentiles.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled in spirit to testify to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
When they opposed him and spoke abusively, he shook out his clothes and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
He left there and entered the house of a man named Titus Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was near the synagogue.
Crispus, the synagogue leader, believed in the Lord with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul in a vision at night, “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, because I have many people in this city.”
He stayed there for a year and six months, teaching them the word of God.
When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up together against Paul and brought him before the tribunal.
They said, “This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law.”
When Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were a matter of wrongdoing or wicked fraud, Jews, it would be reasonable for me to listen to you.
But if these are disputes about words and names and your own law, see to them yourselves, for I do not wish to be a judge of such matters.”
He drove them away from the tribunal.
All the Greeks seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the tribunal, but Gallio was not concerned about any of this.
Paul stayed for many more days, then said farewell to the brothers and sailed for Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila. He had his head shaved at Cenchreae, because he had taken a vow.
When he arrived at Ephesus, he left them there, but he himself entered the synagogue and spoke with the Jews.
They asked him to stay there longer, but he did not agree.
Instead, he said farewell to them and said, “I will return to you again, God willing.”
He sailed from Ephesus, landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the church, and went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he set out and traveled through the region of Galatia and Phrygia in turn, strengthening all the disciples.
A Jew named Apelles, an Alexandrian by birth and an eloquent man, arrived at Ephesus. He was well versed in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and, being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Aquila and Priscilla heard him, they took him to themselves and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
When he wished to go to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived there, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace.
For he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the inland regions and went down to Ephesus, where he found some disciples.
He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
He said, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Paul said, “John baptized all the people with a baptism of repentance and told them to believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus Christ.”
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
When Paul laid his hand on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
There were about twelve men in all.
He entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, speaking and persuading people about the kingdom of God.
But when some became stubborn and opposed him, speaking against the Way before the crowd, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples, speaking daily in the lecture hall of a certain Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, until all the inhabitants of Asia, both Jews and Gentiles, had heard the word of the Lord.
God performed many mighty works through Paul.
Even handkerchiefs or cloths carrying his sweat were taken to the sick, and their illnesses left them and the evil spirits came out.
Some of the traveling Jewish exorcists also dared to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.”
