There were seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who were doing this.
The evil spirit answered and said to them, “I know Jesus, and I recognize Paul, but who are you?”
The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped upon them, seized both of them, and overpowered them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Gentiles living in Ephesus. Fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in increasing honor.
Many of those who had believed came, confessing and recounting their deeds.
Many of those who practiced magic brought their books and burned them before everyone. They calculated their value and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.
In this way the word of God grew and became strong.
When these things were completed, Paul resolved to travel through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem. He said, “After I have gone there, I must also see Rome.”
He sent two of his assistants, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed in Asia for some time.
At that time there arose a considerable disturbance concerning the Way.
A silversmith named Demetrius made silver shrines of the deity Artemis and brought considerable profit to the craftsmen.
He gathered them together, along with the workers in that trade, and said, “Men, you yourselves know that we make our profit from this work.
And you see and hear that this Paul has persuaded and turned away large crowds, not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia, saying that things made by human hands are not gods.

And not only is our trade in danger of falling into disrepute, but the temple of the great goddess Artemis may also be regarded as nothing, and her greatness may even be destroyed—she whom all Asia and the whole world worship.
When they heard this, they were filled with anger and shouted, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The city was filled with confusion. They rushed together into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s traveling companions.
When Paul wanted to go into the crowd, the disciples would not let him.
Some of the officials of Asia, who were his friends, sent word to him and begged him not to venture into the theater.
Some shouted one thing and others another, for their assembly was in confusion, and many of them did not know why they had gathered.
They brought Alexander forward from the crowd, and when the Jews had brought him forward, Alexander motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defense before the crowd.
When they learned that the man was a Jew, they all shouted with one voice for about two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

The city clerk quieted the crowd and said, “Men of Ephesus, who among people does not know that the city of the Ephesians is adorned with the temple of the great goddess Artemis and of the image that fell from heaven?
Since this is beyond doubt, you must remain calm and do nothing rash.
You have brought these men here, although they are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, let them go to court. There are judges, and they can bring charges against one another.
But if there is an inquiry concerning anything else, it shall be settled in a lawful assembly.”

For we are also in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, though there is no cause for it, and we will not be able to give an account of this gathering.’ After saying this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the crowd had quieted down, Paul called the disciples, encouraged them, said farewell, and left for Macedonia.
After traveling through those regions and encouraging them with many words, he came to Greece.
When he had spent three months there, the Jews plotted against him as he was about to leave for Syria, so he decided to return through Macedonia.
Sosipater, son of Pyrrhus, from Berea, accompanied him as far as Asia, along with Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius from Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
These men went ahead and waited for us in Troas.
After the days of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi and came to them in Troas within five days. We stayed there seven days.
On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul spoke with them, since he was going to leave the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the windowsill, sinking into a deep sleep. As Paul continued speaking at length, he was overcome by sleep and fell down from the third story. He was picked up dead.
Paul went down, threw himself upon him, took him in his arms, and said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is still in him.”
He went upstairs, broke bread and ate, and spoke for a long time until dawn. Then he left.
They brought the young man back alive and were greatly comforted.
We boarded the ship and set sail for Assos, where we intended to take Paul aboard again, for he had arranged it this way, intending to travel overland himself.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mytilene.
Sailing from there, the next day we arrived opposite Chios. The following day we reached Samos, and the day after that we came to Miletus.
For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not spend any time lingering in Asia, because he was hurrying to reach Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, if that were possible for him.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the church.
When they came to him, he said to them, ‘You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time, from the first day I came to Asia.’
Serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
How I did not hold back from telling you anything useful and teaching you publicly and from house to house.
Testifying to Jews and Gentiles about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, look, bound in spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there.
Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city and says, “Chains and hardships await you.”
But I do not consider my life precious at all, so that I may finish my course with joy and complete the service I received from the Lord Jesus: to testify to the good news of God’s grace.
And now, look, I know that none of you among whom I went about preaching the kingdom of God will see my face again.
Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of everyone's blood.
For I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole will of God.
Watch over yourselves and the whole flock, among whom the Holy Spirit has appointed you as overseers, to shepherd the Lord's people, whom he redeemed with his own blood.
For I know that after my departure, ravenous wolves will come among you and will not spare the flock.
And from among you men will arise who will speak distorted things to draw the disciples away after themselves.
Therefore stay alert, and remember that for three years, night and day, I did not stop admonishing each one of you with tears.
And now I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all the holy ones.
I coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing among you.
You yourselves know that these hands provided for my needs and the needs of those who were with me.
In everything I showed you that we must work in this way and support the sick, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, who himself said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
When he had said this, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
They all wept greatly, threw their arms around Paul's neck, and kissed him.
They grieved most of all over his statement that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
When we had set sail and parted from them, we went straight to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Finding a ship bound for Phoenicia, we boarded it and set sail.
When Cyprus came into view, we left it on our left and sailed to Syria, landing at Tyre, because the ship was to unload its cargo there.
We found the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
When our days there were over, we set out, and everyone, together with their wives and children, accompanied us outside the city. We knelt on the seashore and prayed.
We said farewell to one another and boarded the ship, and they returned to their own homes.
And after we had [?] the ship from Tyre, we reached Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left there and came to Caesarea. We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who were prophets.
While we were staying there for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “This is what the Holy Spirit says: The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt in this way and hand him over to the Gentiles.”
When we heard this, we and the people there begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, ‘What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.’
When he would not listen, we fell silent, saying, “Let the Lord's will be done.”
After those days, we made preparations and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us and brought us to Mnason, a Cypriot and an early disciple, with whom we were to stay.
When we entered Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us joyfully.
The next day Paul went with us to James, and all the elders came.
After greeting them, he recounted one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard this, they glorified God and said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of Jews have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
But they have been informed about you that you teach all the Jews living among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or follow the customs.
What, then, is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
So do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow upon themselves.

Take them, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing to what they have been told about you, but that you too conform to the law and keep it.

But concerning the Gentiles who have believed, we sent word, according to our decision, that they should observe no such thing, but only abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

Then Paul took the men, and the next day, after purifying himself with them, he entered the temple to announce the completion of the days of purification, until an offering was presented for each of them.
When the seven days were nearly over, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd against him, laid hands on him, and shouted,
“Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law, and this place. He has even brought Gentiles into the temple and defiled this holy place.”
For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city and supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, and the people gathered together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, news reached the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in turmoil.
He immediately took soldiers and centurions and rushed down to them. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the commander approached, seized him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing about him, and others another. Since he could not learn the truth because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks.
When he reached the steps, the soldiers had to lift him up and carry him because of the crowd’s violence.
For the mass of people followed, shouting, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be taken into the barracks, he said to the commander, “May I speak to you?” He replied, “Do you know Greek?
Are you not the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a rebellion and led four thousand assassins out into the wilderness?”
Paul said, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he gave permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the people with his hand. When a deep silence fell, he began speaking in the Hebrew language, saying:
“Brothers and fathers, listen now to the defense I make before you.”
When they heard him speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter.

He said, “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city. At the feet of Gamaliel I was instructed strictly according to the law of our ancestors. I was zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prison,

as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify about me. From them I also received letters to the brothers, and I was traveling to Damascus to bring those there in chains to Jerusalem to be punished.
As I traveled and approached Damascus around noon, a bright light from heaven suddenly flashed around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’
Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me.
I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told everything you are commanded to do.’
Since I could not see because of the brilliance of that light, those who were with me led me by the hand, and I entered Damascus.
A man named Ananias, devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living in Damascus,
came and stood beside me and said, ‘Brother Saul, regain your sight.’

At that very moment I regained my sight and looked at him. He said to me, ‘The God of our ancestors chose you beforehand to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth.
For you will be his witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now why do you delay? Get up, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’
When I returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
and saw him saying to me, “Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.”
And I said, “Lord, they themselves know that I used to imprison and beat those who believed in you in the synagogues.
And when the blood of your witness Stephen was being shed, I myself stood there, approved of his killing, and guarded the clothes of those who killed him.”
And he said to me, “Go, because I will send you far away to the Gentiles.”
They listened to him until he said this. Then they raised their voices and said, “Rid the earth of such a man! Someone like him ought not to live!”
As they shouted, threw off their clothes, and tossed dust into the air,
the commander ordered him to be brought into the barracks. He said to interrogate him by flogging: “So that I may find out what offense has made them shout against him like this.”
When they stretched him out with straps, Paul said to the centurion standing nearby, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen who has not been found guilty?”
When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander, reported it, and said, “What do you intend to do? This man is a Roman citizen.”
The commander came over and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.”
The commander replied, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum of money.” Paul said, “But I was born with it.”
Those who were about to beat him immediately withdrew from him. The commander himself was afraid when he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had already bound him.
The next day, wanting to learn the truth about the Jews’ accusation, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the entire council to assemble. He brought Paul down and stood him among them.
Paul looked intently at the council and said, “Brothers, I have lived before God with an entirely clear conscience to this day.”
The high priest Ananias ordered the attendants to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there to judge me according to the law, yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck!”
Those standing around him said, “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”
Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people.’”

When Paul realized that one side consisted of Sadducees and the other of Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee. I am being tried because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead.”
When he said this, a dispute arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.
For the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor any angel or spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge both.
There was a great uproar. Some of the scribes on the Pharisees’ side stood up and argued, saying, “We find nothing wrong with this man. But what if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?”
As the uproar increased, the commander feared that Paul might be torn apart by them. He ordered the soldiers to go down, seize him from among them, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night the Lord stood beside him and said, “Take courage, Paul. Just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”
When morning came, the Jews gathered together and bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty who had made this oath together.
They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have bound ourselves under a curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
Now you, together with the council, notify the commander to bring him down to you, as though you wanted to learn more precisely about him. We are ready to kill him before he comes near.”
When Paul’s sister’s son heard about the plot, he came into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions to him and said, “Take this young man to the commander, for he has something to tell him.”
He took him to the commander and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.”
The commander took him by the hand, went aside, and asked, “What do you have to tell me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they wanted to inquire more precisely about him.

Do not listen to them, for more than forty of their men are lying in wait for him. They have bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are now ready and waiting for your order.”
Then the commander dismissed the young man, instructing him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of this.”
He called two of the centurions and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, along with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, at the third hour of the night.
And have mounts ready, so that they may bring Paul down and take him safely to Felix the governor.”
He wrote a letter that read as follows:
“Claudius Lysias, to the excellent governor Felix: Greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them. I came upon them with soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.
I wanted to know the offense for which they were accusing him, so I brought him down to their council.
I found that he was being accused over a question about their laws, but he had committed no offense deserving death or imprisonment.
When I was informed of a plot they were planning against this man, I sent him to you, also ordering his accusers to speak against him before you. Farewell.”
The soldiers, following his orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
The next day, they sent the horsemen on with him and returned to the barracks.
They entered Caesarea, delivered the letter to the governor, and also presented Paul before him.
When he had read it, he asked what province he was from and learned that he was from Cilicia.
“I will hear you,” he said, “when your accusers also arrive.” And he ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod’s palace.
After five days, the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and an orator named Tertullus, and they presented their case against Paul to the governor.
When he was called, Tertullus began to make his accusation, saying, “We have enjoyed great peace through you, and affairs have been put right for this nation through your care.
In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we acknowledge this with complete gratitude.
But so that I may not trouble you any further, I ask you, in your kindness, to hear us briefly.”
For we found this man to be a corrupter and a troublemaker among all the Jews throughout the world, and a leader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even tried to desecrate the temple. We arrested him and wanted to judge him according to our laws.
But Lysias the commander came and took him out of our hands with great force.
He ordered his accusers to come before you. By examining him again yourself, you will be able to learn about everything of which we accuse him.
The Jews also joined in, saying, “That is so.”
When the governor motioned to him to speak, Paul answered: “I know that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, so I gladly give an answer concerning my case.
You can ascertain that it has been no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
They did not find me in the temple arguing with anyone or gathering a crowd, nor in the synagogues.
Neither in the city; nor can they prove to you the things they now accuse me of.
But I confess this to you: according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our ancestors, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets.
I have hope in God, which they themselves also hold, that there will be a resurrection of the righteous and of sinners.
For this reason I too strive always to keep a clear conscience before God and people.
After many years, I came to bring charitable gifts to my nation and offered sacrifices.
During these things they found me purified in the temple, without a crowd or a disturbance.
There were some Jews from Asia who ought to appear before you and bring charges if they have anything against me.
Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me while I stood before the council,
except for this one statement that I shouted while [?] stood among them: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged by you today.’”
Felix postponed their case, since he had more exact knowledge of the Way. He said, “When Lysias the commander comes down here, I will investigate your case.”
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but allow him some freedom, and not to prevent any of his own people from attending to him.
After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He summoned Paul and heard him speak about faith in Jesus Christ.
As Paul spoke about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and answered, “Go away for now. When I have time, I will summon you.”
At the same time he hoped that Paul would give him something, so he frequently summoned him and talked with him.
When two years had passed, Porcius Festus succeeded Felix. Wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul imprisoned.
Three days after Festus arrived to take office, he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the leaders of the Jews brought their case against Paul to him.
They pleaded with him, asking him for the favor of summoning Paul to Jerusalem, while arranging an ambush to kill him on the road.
But Festus answered that Paul was being held in Caesarea and that he himself would be going there soon.
“Let those among you who have authority,” he said, “go down with me, and if there is anything wrong with this man, let them bring charges against him.”
After staying there no more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they could not prove.
Paul answered in his defense, “I have done nothing wrong against the law of the Jews, against the temple, or against Caesar.”
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there before me concerning these matters?”
Paul said, “I stand before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done the Jews no wrong, as you yourself know very well.

If I am guilty and have done anything deserving death, I do not shrink from dying. But if there is nothing to the charges these men bring against me, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”
Then Festus, after conferring with his council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go.”
After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea to greet Festus.
While they were spending many days there, Festus told the king about Paul, saying, “There is a man here whom Felix left in prison.
When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the leaders of the Jews brought his case to my attention and asked me to punish him.
I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to hand anyone over as a favor before the accused has faced his accusers and has had an opportunity to answer the accusation.
So when they came here, I made no delay, but the next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought in.
When his accusers came forward, they brought no charge of wrongdoing of the kind I had expected.
Instead, they had some disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul said was alive.
Being at a loss as to how to investigate such matters, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there concerning these matters.
But when Paul appealed to be held for a hearing before Augustus, I ordered him to be kept in custody until I could have him sent to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I too would like to hear the man.” He replied, “Tomorrow you shall hear him.”
The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall with the military commanders and the prominent men of the city. At Festus’s command, Paul was brought in.

Festus said, “King Agrippa and all you men who are here with us, do you see this man? The whole assembly of the Jews brought accusations against him before me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live.
But I found that he had done nothing deserving death, and since he himself appealed to Augustus, I decided to send him.

I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. For that reason I have brought him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after further examination I may have something to write.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner without indicating the charges against him.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak on your own behalf.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:
“Concerning all the accusations the Jews bring against me, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate that I am to make my defense before you today.
Especially because you are well acquainted with all the customs and disputes of the Jews, I beg you to listen to me patiently.
For all the Jews know about my life from childhood, which I lived from the beginning among my own nation in Jerusalem.
They have known me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, and know that I lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest observance of our law.
And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to the fathers.
Our twelve tribes hope to attain this promise by worshiping unceasingly night and day. It is because of this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews.
Why does it seem unbelievable to you that God raises the dead?
I myself thought it right to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is just what I did in Jerusalem. Having received authority from the chief priests, I imprisoned many of the saints, and when they were put to death, I cast my vote against them.
I punished them often in every synagogue and tried to force them to blaspheme. In my increasing rage against them, I pursued them even to foreign cities.
For this purpose I went to Damascus with authority and orders from the chief priests.
At midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the radiance of the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.
When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”
And I said, “Who are you, Lord?” And the Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”

“But rise and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and a witness to the things in which you have seen me and those in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from this people and from the Gentiles, to whom I will send you,
to open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a share among those sanctified by faith in me.”
Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.

But I proclaimed first to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, and throughout all the regions of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to the living God, doing deeds worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and wanted to kill me.
Having received help from God, I have stood to this day, testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen:
that Christ would suffer and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.
As he gave this defense, Festus said in a loud voice, “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is driving you mad.”
But Paul said, “I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking words of sound judgment and truth.
The king knows about these things, and I speak freely with him. For I do not believe that any of these things are hidden from you, since this was not done in some corner.
Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”
And Agrippa said to Paul, “You almost persuade me to become a Christian.”
And Paul said, “I would pray to God that, whether with little or much, not only you but also everyone listening to me today might become as I am, except for these chains.”
The king stood up, along with the governor, Bernice, and those seated with them.
As they left, they spoke to one another and said, “This man is doing nothing deserving death or imprisonment.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
When orders were given for us to sail to Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan regiment.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was going to the regions of Asia and set sail. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was also with us.
The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius showed kindness to Paul and allowed him to go to his friends and receive care.
Setting out from there, we sailed in the shelter of Cyprus because the wind was against us.
Then we sailed across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and landed at Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy and put us aboard it.
We sailed slowly for many days and barely reached Cnidus. Since the wind would not let us proceed, we sailed in the shelter of Crete, off Salmone.
With difficulty we passed it and came to a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
Much time had passed, and sailing had become dangerous, especially since the Fast was already over. Paul gave them advice
and said to them, “Men, I see that this voyage will bring hardship and great loss, not only to the cargo and the ship, but also to our lives.”
But the centurion paid more attention to the captain and the pilot than to Paul's words.

Since the harbor seemed unsuitable for spending the winter, most decided to leave there, hoping they might reach Phoenix and spend the winter in that harbor of Crete, which faced toward the south and toward the land.
When the south wind began to blow, they thought they could reach their intended destination. They set out and sailed close along Crete.
Not long afterward, a violent wind called Euroclydon swept down upon it.
The ship was caught and could not withstand the wind, so we gave way and drifted to and fro.
Making for an island called Clauda, we barely managed to secure the boat.
After taking it aboard, they used supports to bind the ship together. Fearing that they might fall into the whirlpool, they lowered the sail and drifted to and fro.
As we were being battered more severely, the next day they began throwing the cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship's equipment overboard with their own hands.
For many days neither sun nor stars appeared, and a severe storm continued to batter us. Then all hope of our being saved began to disappear.
Since they had gone hungry for many days, Paul stood among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not left Crete, and thus avoided this hardship and loss.
And now I urge you to take courage, because none of you will lose your life; only the ship will be lost.
For this night an angel of God, to whom I belong and whom I worship, appeared to me
and said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must also stand before Caesar, and look, God has granted you all those who are with you aboard the ship.’
Therefore take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen just as he told me.
But we must run aground on some island.
When the fourteenth night came, while we were being tossed about in the depths of the Adriatic, around midnight the sailors thought they were approaching some land.
They lowered the sounding weights and found twenty fathoms. After a short interval they lowered them again and found fifteen fathoms.
Afraid that they might run aground somewhere on rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and longed for daybreak.
But the sailors were trying to escape from the ship. They lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they were going to put out anchors from the bow.
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut the boat’s ropes and let it fall away.
As daybreak approached, Paul urged everyone to take food, saying, “This is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting, remaining without food and eating nothing.
Therefore I urge you to eat some food, for this is necessary for your survival. Not a hair from the head of any of you will be lost.”
When he had said this, he took bread, thanked God before them all, broke it, and began to eat.
And they were all encouraged, and they too took food.
There were two hundred and seventy-six of us altogether on the ship.
When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach. They considered whether they could bring the ship safely ashore there.
They cut off the anchors and dropped them into the sea, loosened the ropes securing the rudders, raised the sail to the wind, and headed toward the shore.
Coming upon a place where two seas met, they ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and remained immovable, while the stern was breaking apart under the pounding.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so that no one could swim away and escape.
But the centurion, wanting to save Paul, prevented them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land,
and the rest to follow, some on planks and some on other equipment from the ship. And so everyone reached land safely.
Once we had escaped safely, we learned that the island was called Melitene. The natives showed us no small kindness.
For they lit a fire and welcomed all of us because of the rain that was coming down and because of the cold.
As Paul gathered a large bundle of brushwood and put it on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “This man must be a murderer. Although he escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm.
They expected him to swell up or fall down and suddenly die. But after waiting a long time and seeing that no harm had come to him, they changed what they were saying and said that he was a god.
Around that place were estates belonging to the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius. He welcomed us and kindly entertained us for three days.
Publius’s father was lying ill with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hand on him, and healed him.
After this happened, the other sick people on the island came and were healed.
They also honored us greatly, and when we departed, they gave us what we needed.
After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island, bearing the emblem of the Dioscuri.
We landed at Syracuse and stayed for three days.
From there we sailed on and reached Rhegium. After one day, a south wind began to blow, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.
There we found brothers who asked us to stay for seven days, and then we went on to Rome.
The brothers there heard about us and came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
When we entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself with the soldier who guarded him.

After three days he called together the Jewish leaders. When they came, he said to them, “Brothers, although I had done nothing against our people or our ancestral customs, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans.
After examining me, they wanted to release me, because they found no offense in me deserving death.
But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not because I had any accusation to bring against my own nation.”
For this reason I asked to see you and speak with you, because it is for the hope of Israel that I am in these chains.
They said to him, “We have received no letters about you from Judea, nor has any brother come and reported or said anything bad about you.
But we ask to hear from you what you think, because we know that this sect is opposed everywhere.”

They appointed a day to meet with him, and many came to him at his lodging. From morning until evening he explained the kingdom of God to them and bore witness to it, seeking to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were persuaded by what he said, while others did not believe.
Disagreeing among themselves, they began to leave after Paul said this one thing: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers,
saying, ‘Go to this people and say: You will hear and hear, but not understand; you will look and look, but not see.

For the heart of this people has grown dull. Their ears are hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, so that they may never see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’
Therefore, let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles. They will listen.”
When he said this, the Jews went away from him, having much debate among themselves.
He stayed for two full years in his own rented lodging.
He welcomed everyone who came to him.
He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without hindrance.
